### Proposed working group name

Agentic Routers and Gateways

### One-sentence summary (elevator pitch, ~25 words max)

A vendor-neutral forum defining shared architecture, interfaces and conformance tests for the routers and gateways between AI agents and their models, tools and other agents.

### Detailed description of the working group's focus and scope

Almost every production agent deployment routes its traffic through an intermediary: agent-to-LLM calls, agent-to-tool calls over MCP, and agent-to-agent calls over A2A. That router or gateway handles routing and failover, authentication and credential brokering, policy enforcement, rate limits, cost attribution, tool filtering and telemetry. This WG defines that layer in common, so that any gateway can work with any agent stack and enterprises can compare, combine and swap implementations.

The WG will cover:
- A reference architecture (layer model) for agent routers and gateways: data plane, control plane, registry/catalog, policy decision and enforcement, credential brokering, usage accounting, telemetry export, and deployment patterns (central, sidecar/mesh, edge, embedded).
- Intermediary behavior profiles for MCP, A2A and LLM APIs: what a conformant gateway must, should and must not do when proxying each protocol.
- Vendor-neutral interfaces between gateways and adjacent systems (external authorization, usage/cost attribution, registry lookup).
- An open, implementation-agnostic conformance test suite and interoperability events.

The WG will not:
- Build, host, endorse, rank or benchmark any gateway. It writes specs and tests, and implementations stay in their own projects.
- Define security benchmarks or threat models (Security & Privacy WG), trace/metric schemas (Observability & Traceability WG, OpenTelemetry), or identity and delegation protocols (Identity & Trust WG). It applies their outputs at the gateway.
- Define Kubernetes-specific APIs (Kubernetes WG AI Gateway / Gateway API Inference Extension), or work on model serving or inference scheduling.
- Change MCP or A2A directly. Proposals go to the protocol maintainers through their own processes.

### Problem statement — what challenge or gap does this address?

The gateway/router has become a de facto layer of the agentic stack, but nothing defines it in common:
- No shared layer model. Each implementation splits data plane, control plane, registry, policy and credential handling differently. Enterprises can't compare products, mix components, or replace one gateway with another without re-plumbing.
- Intermediary behavior is undefined in the protocols. MCP and A2A were designed mainly for direct client-to-server connections. What a proxy must preserve, may change or must reject (sessions, streaming, tool lists, auth headers, errors) is left to each implementer, so the same agent can behave differently behind different gateways.
- No common interfaces to the surrounding systems. Every gateway builds its own bespoke integrations with policy engines, identity providers, billing/usage systems and registries.
- No conformance baseline shows that a gateway handles MCP, A2A and LLM traffic correctly.
- 

Why no existing body covers it:
- AAIF WGs each own a cross-cutting concern (security, observability, identity, reliability, governance). None owns the gateway as a component, or the interfaces between it and the systems around it.
- AAIF-hosted gateway projects (agentgateway, Agent Router) govern their own code. A project can't be the neutral venue for specs that its peers must also implement.
- Kubernetes WG AI Gateway / Gateway API Inference Extension focus on running gateways on Kubernetes and on inference-aware routing for self-hosted models. Their charter excludes building whole AI gateway solutions, and neither covers MCP/A2A or works outside Kubernetes.
- No standards body covers how agent-protocol intermediaries behave across LLM, MCP and A2A traffic together.

### Why is this relevant to Agentic AI specifically?

Traditional API gateways manage stateless request/response traffic between known services. 

Agent traffic is different:
- Dynamic, model-chosen calls. An agent decides at runtime which tools and agents to call, so the gateway is where tool exposure, filtering and authorization have to happen.
- Stateful, long-running protocols. MCP sessions, streaming and A2A tasks break assumptions that existing gateway standards rely on.
- Delegated identity. Calls are made on behalf of users through chains of agents, so the gateway must carry and enforce delegated identity, not just authenticate a client.
- Token-metered cost. Spend is per token and per model, so attribution to user, team, agent and project is a gateway responsibility.
- Multi-hop traces. One user request fans out across models, tools and agents, and the gateway is the natural correlation point.

### Proposed goals and intended outcomes

1. A shared vocabulary and layer model that AAIF projects, members and enterprises use to describe agent gateways (measured by adoption in AAIF project docs and member reference architectures).
2. Consistent agent behavior behind any conformant gateway for MCP, A2A and LLM traffic (measured by published intermediary profiles and conformance results).
3. One integration target per adjacent system (policy, usage/cost, registry) instead of one per gateway vendor (measured by interface specs adopted by at least two implementations).
4. A conformance suite that at least two independent gateways run and publish results against within the first year.
5. Feedback loop to the protocols: gateway-relevant issues filed with, and resolved by, MCP and A2A maintainers.

### How does this align with the Agentic AI Foundation's mission?

AAIF exists to provide neutral, open governance so that agentic systems interoperate. It already hosts the protocols (MCP, with A2A alongside in the ecosystem) and two gateway projects with different designs: agentgateway and Agent Router. This WG ties them together. It makes the protocols work predictably through intermediaries, and it gives every gateway, hosted or not, open source or commercial, a neutral place to agree on interfaces. Having several hosted gateways then becomes a strength, and AAIF becomes the place where the agent traffic layer is defined, not just where implementations live. This also supports the Foundation's enterprise-scale priority: gateways are where enterprises apply security, governance, observability and cost control to agents.

### Key topics or workstreams to be covered

- Architecture & Interfaces: reference architecture/layer model, deployment patterns, and gateway-to-ecosystem interfaces (external authorization/policy decision, usage and cost attribution records, registry/catalog lookup).
- Protocol Profiles & Conformance: intermediary behavior profiles for MCP, A2A and LLM APIs, the conformance test suite, and interoperability events.
- Liaison (cross-cutting): coordination with the Security & Privacy, Observability & Traceability, Identity & Trust, Accuracy & Reliability and Taxonomy & Landscape groups, MCP/A2A maintainers, and Kubernetes WG AI Gateway.

### Proposed deliverables (e.g., whitepaper, standards, guidelines, tooling)


Deliverable | Type | Intended users | What "complete" looks like
-- | -- | -- | --
Landscape survey + glossary terms | Report | WG, Taxonomy & Landscape WG, enterprises | Published survey of hosted and external gateway/router implementations, with terms contributed to the AAIF glossary
Reference Architecture v1.0 | Whitepaper | Architects, platform teams, implementers | Layer model and deployment patterns approved by WG consensus and reviewed by both hosted gateway projects
MCP Intermediary Profile | Specification | Gateway implementers, MCP maintainers | v1.0 published, gateway-relevant MCP issues filed
A2A and LLM-API Intermediary Profiles | Specification | Gateway implementers, A2A maintainers | v0.9 drafts out for public review
Interface specs: external authorization, usage/cost attribution | Specification | Gateway, policy-engine and billing/FinOps vendors | v0.9 drafts, each prototyped by at least two implementations
Conformance test suite v0.1 | Tooling (open source) | Implementers, enterprise buyers | Covers the MCP profile, with results published for at least two gateways (target: agentgateway and Agent Router, plus volunteers)
Interoperability event | Demo/plugfest | Community, enterprises | Multi-gateway demo at an AAIF/MCP Dev Summit



### First-year delivery timeline

First 6 months: landscape survey, Reference Architecture v1.0, and a draft MCP intermediary profile; by month 12: A2A/LLM profile and interface spec drafts, conformance suite v0.1 run on 2+ gateways, and an interop demo.

### Suggested meeting cadence

Biweekly, 60 min, open meetings with published notes; async work on GitHub and AAIF Discord; workstream sub-calls as needed from month 3.

- Gateway and router implementers: maintai- Gateway and router implementers: maintainers of agentgateway and Agent Router, plus other open source and commercial gateway, API-management and service-mesh vendors.
- Protocol experts: MCP and A2A maintainers and contributors.
- Enterprise platform operators running agents in production (financial services, telecom, retail, public sector), who supply requirements and validate the reference architecture.
- Adjacent-system vendors: policy/authorization engines, identity providers, observability and FinOps/billing platforms.
- Cloud and Kubernetes platform providers, including liaison to Kubernetes WG AI Gateway.
- Conformance and testing expertise for the test suite.

### Ideal working group size

15-25 active contributors from at least 8 organizations; participation open to all

### Overlap and coordination with AAIF WGs and external bodies

Neutral ground for all gateways. No single implementation's architecture becomes the reference, every spec must be implementable by more than one project, and the chair and co-chair come from different organizations, neither of which is the primary maintainer of a hosted gateway project. Each hosted gateway project is invited to review every draft before it advances.

AAIF-hosted projects
- agentgateway: equal standing with every other implementation. Its maintainers are invited as participants and early conformance implementers. The WG does not direct its roadmap.
- Agent Router: same as above. Its Envoy-based design (control plane over a proven data plane) is a different architectural point, which helps keep the reference architecture implementation-neutral.
- MCP: the WG documents intermediary requirements and proposes changes through MCP's own process. It never forks or extends the protocol.
- A2A: same approach as MCP. We send intermediary requirements through its own process.

AAIF working groups
- Security & Privacy: they set security-by-design practices, benchmarks and adversarial testing across agentic systems. We apply them at the gateway as an enforcement point, adopt their benchmarks into gateway profiles, and hand gateway-specific threats back to them. A liaison attends both groups.
- Observability & Traceability: they own tracing, correlation, audit and metric schemas. We specify only where and when gateways emit telemetry and which context they propagate, using their schemas as-is.
- Identity & Trust: they define agent identity and delegation. We specify how gateways carry, exchange and enforce it, with joint review of the authorization and credential-brokering interfaces.
- Accuracy & Reliability: we align gateway retry and failover semantics with their recovery definitions.
- Taxonomy & Landscape: we contribute gateway terms and the landscape survey.

External bodies

- Kubernetes SIG Network (WG AI Gateway, Gateway API Inference Extension): complementary. They cover Kubernetes deployment and inference routing, while we cover protocol-level behavior on any platform. We'll align terms and offer our profiles as a reference.
- OpenTelemetry (GenAI semantic conventions): source of telemetry schemas, via the Observability & Traceability WG.
- IETF / OpenID Foundation: existing OAuth and token-exchange standards are reused for credential brokering, not reinvented.
- OWASP GenAI Security Project, CoSAI: threat guidance, used through the Security & Privacy WG.

### Who are the primary beneficiaries of this work?

Enterprises and platform teams deploying agents, who get portability between gateways, the ability to mix components, and a conformance baseline to buy against.
Gateway and router implementers (open source and commercial), who get one integration target per adjacent system and a neutral venue for resolving protocol ambiguities.
Agent and tool developers, whose agents and MCP servers behave the same behind any conformant gateway.
MCP and A2A maintainers, who get consolidated, implementation-tested intermediary requirements.
Adjacent-system vendors (policy, identity, observability, FinOps), who integrate once instead of per gateway.

### Anticipated impact (technical / policy / industry / societal)

Technical: a common layer model, predictable protocol behavior through intermediaries, and reusable interfaces and conformance tests. This reduces integration work across the ecosystem.
Industry: lowers lock-in and switching costs, lets several gateway projects coexist and compete on quality rather than on proprietary interfaces, and gives buyers a conformance signal.
Policy: gateways are where enterprises enforce governance and regulatory controls on agents. Standard enforcement points and audit hooks make it easier to apply the Governance, Risk & Regulatory Alignment and Security & Privacy WGs' frameworks in practice.
Societal: consistent, auditable control points for agent actions (who acted, on whose behalf, with which tools, at what cost) support safer and more accountable agent deployment.

### Urgency — why now?

AAIF now hosts two gateway projects with different architectures (agentgateway, approved May 2026, and Agent Router, joined September 2026), and more implementations are emerging.
Enterprises are standardizing their agent traffic layer now. Interfaces agreed in the next 12 months will shape the market, and interfaces agreed later will have to reconcile entrenched divergence.
MCP and A2A are still evolving. Intermediary requirements are much cheaper to address in the protocols now than after they stabilize.
Without a neutral venue, gateway convergence will happen through vendor competition rather than open interfaces, which runs counter to AAIF's purpose.

### Are there risks or challenges to this working group succeeding?


Risk | Mitigation
-- | --
Perceived as a vehicle for one vendor's or project's architecture | Chairs from different organizations, neither the primary maintainer of a hosted gateway. Multi-implementation rule for every spec. Every hosted gateway project reviews each draft.
Hosted gateway maintainers don't engage | Invited early as conformance implementers, keep demands on their roadmaps minimal, and make conformance results visibly useful to their adopters.
Scope creep into security, observability or identity | Explicit out-of-scope list. Named liaisons to the relevant WGs. Use their outputs as-is.
Specs that nobody implements | Every interface spec needs at least two prototype implementations before v1.0, and conformance tests ship alongside the specs.
MCP/A2A churn invalidates profiles | Version profiles against protocol releases and coordinate with maintainers on their roadmaps.
Volunteer bandwidth | Narrow year-one deliverables, two workstreams, and committed contributors from at least three organizations at launch.



### Estimated resource needs (budget, tooling, staff support)

Staff: standard AAIF WG support (scheduling, recordings and notes, mailing list/Discord channel).
Tooling: one GitHub repository for specs and the conformance suite. Modest CI capacity for conformance runs, which participants can donate.
Budget: none beyond optional space at an existing AAIF/MCP Dev Summit for the interoperability event.
